subject: biology
title: Required practical: osmosis in plant tissue
key_idea: In this practical, pieces of potato are left in solutions of different concentrations and weighed before and after. Water moves in or out by osmosis, so the mass changes. Plotting percentage change in mass against concentration shows the concentration at which there is no change.

blocks.text: Potato cells have a partially permeable membrane. Water moves across it by **osmosis**. If the solution outside is more dilute than the cell contents, the potato gains water and its mass goes up. If the solution outside is more concentrated, the potato loses water and its mass goes down.

If the solution has the same concentration as the cell contents, there is no overall movement of water. The mass stays the same. This lets you find the concentration of the solution inside the potato cells.

rows: The concentration of the salt or sugar solution
The mass of the potato piece, used to find the percentage change in mass
Same type of potato, no skin, same size and mass of piece, same volume of solution, same time in the solution, same temperature, same solute

diagram.alt: Seven steps in order: cut equal potato pieces, weigh each piece, put each piece in a different concentration, leave for the same time, blot dry and reweigh, calculate percentage change, plot a graph.

items.text: Use the same potato. Remove the skin, because water cannot move through it. Cut pieces of the same size, for example cylinders cut with a cork borer.
Label a tube or beaker for each concentration. Use a range of at least five, including 0.0 mol/dm³ (distilled water). Put the same volume of solution in each, enough to cover the piece.
Dry each piece on a paper towel. Weigh it on a balance and record the starting mass.
Put one piece in each tube. Make sure each is fully submerged. Keep them all at the same temperature.
Leave the pieces for the same time, at least 10 minutes. Longer gives larger changes.
Remove each piece and blot it dry in the same way. Weigh it and record the final mass.
Do each concentration at least three times so that you can calculate a mean.

blocks.text: Blotting dry is important. Water left on the surface would add to the mass and give a false result.
Work out the change in mass for each piece. Then work out the **percentage change in mass**. This allows pieces with different starting masses to be compared.
percentage change in mass = (change in mass ÷ mass at the start) × 100

For example, a piece goes from 7.96 g to 8.21 g. The change is 0.25 g. 0.25 ÷ 7.96 × 100 = 3.14%. A gain is a positive percentage. A loss is a negative percentage, written with a minus sign. Round to the number of significant figures the question asks for.
Calculate the mean percentage change at each concentration. An **anomalous result** is one that does not fit the pattern. Do not include it in the mean.

Plot a line graph with concentration on the x axis and mean percentage change on the y axis. Draw a line of best fit. The line crosses zero where the piece neither gains nor loses mass. At this concentration the solution outside has the same concentration as the solution inside the potato cells.
If the points are not close enough to read this value, repeat with more concentrations close to the point where the line crosses zero.

A result is **repeatable** if the same person gets the same result when they repeat the experiment. A result is **reproducible** if a different person, or different equipment or method, gives the same result. Repeating readings also helps to spot anomalous results.

items: Use more concentrations so that the point of no change can be found more precisely.
Use a balance with a smaller resolution, so that small changes in mass can be measured.
Use the same potato, with the skin removed, and pieces of the same size.
Keep the time in the solution and the temperature the same.
A control using boiled potato shows no change in mass. Boiling damages the membrane, so it is no longer partially permeable.

blocks.text: Excess liquid left on a piece is a random error, because it changes from piece to piece. A balance that is not calibrated correctly is a systematic error, because every reading is wrong in the same way.

checks.q: Why is each piece of potato blotted dry before it is weighed?
checks.a: Water on the surface would increase the mass, so the mass of the potato alone would not be measured.

checks.q: Why is percentage change in mass calculated rather than just the change in mass?
checks.a: The pieces have different starting masses. Percentage change takes this into account so the results can be compared.

checks.q: A potato piece has a mass of 7.96 g at the start and 8.21 g at the end. Calculate the percentage change in mass to 3 significant figures.

blot the potato pieces dry

the concentration where the line crosses zero percentage change
the membrane was damaged or leaky

mistakes.wrong: The size of the potato was a control variable.
mistakes.right: "Size of potato" is ignored. Say the size of the piece of potato, the type of potato, the volume of solution, or the time the pieces are left in the solution.

mistakes.wrong: The boiled carrot did not change in mass because its cells are dead.
mistakes.right: "Dead cells" is ignored. Say that the membrane was damaged or leaky, so it was no longer partially permeable.

mistakes.wrong: Dry the potato because water left on it would make the mass lower.
mistakes.right: Water left on would make the mass higher or affect it. This answer is not accepted.

worked_example.question:
A student investigated the effect of concentration of salt solution on the mass of uncooked potato pieces.

Plan a method that could be used to obtain results for the effect of salt solution concentration on the mass of uncooked potato pieces.
answer_points: Measure and record the mass of each potato piece.
Place the pieces into different concentrations of salt solution, using at least three concentrations.
Leave the pieces in the solutions for the same time, at least 10 minutes, and at the same temperature.
Remove the pieces from the solutions and blot them dry.
Measure and record the mass again and calculate the change in mass.
Repeat each concentration two more times and calculate the mean change in mass.
Control variables: same size or mass of piece, same potato with no skin, same blotting technique.
worked_example.tip: This is a levelled answer. A full set of steps in a logical order, giving comparable results across concentrations, reaches the top level of 5 to 6 marks.

mistakes.right: Round to the number of significant figures asked for, here 2, giving 19%. Without the rounding the final mark is lost.

mistakes.wrong: Repeat the investigation to make the measurement of mass more accurate.
mistakes.right: Repeating is ignored for accuracy of a mass reading. Dry the piece, or check that the balance reads zero.

mistakes.wrong: Percentage change = change in mass ÷ final mass × 100.
mistakes.right: Divide by the mass at the start. Percentage change = change in mass ÷ mass at the start × 100.

worked_example.question:
A student investigated the movement of water in potatoes.
The student used three identical cubes of potato.
One cube was placed in water and each of the other two cubes were placed in solutions with different concentrations of salt.
The cubes were left for 20 minutes.
The student wanted to find the concentration of salt solution where the potato cube did not change mass.

Describe how the student could modify this investigation to find this concentration.
answer_points: Use concentrations between the dilute and the concentrated solution already used.
Make repeated readings at each concentration and find an average.
Plot a graph and find the concentration where the line crosses the x axis, which is the concentration with no mass change.
Control the other variables, for example temperature.
worked_example.tip: Any three score one mark each.

exam_phrases: use a (measuring) balance
measure the mass of the cube at the start and at the end
blot or dry the outside of the cubes
repeat the experiment / take repeat readings
another student conducts the experiment / use different equipment
the same water potential, so no net water loss or gain
percentage change allows comparison even if the original sizes are different
excess fluid is a random error, an uncalibrated scale is a systematic error

mistakes.wrong: Make the cubes the same mass and measure the volume of the solutions.
mistakes.right: This is ignored when finding percentage change. Use a balance, measure the mass of each cube at the start and at the end, and blot the cubes dry.

mistakes.wrong: To check the data is repeatable and reproducible, compare the results.
mistakes.right: "Compare the results" is ignored. Repeatable: repeat the experiment. Reproducible: another student does it, or different equipment or a different method is used.

mistakes.wrong: The amount of solution is a control variable.
mistakes.right: "Amount of solution" is ignored. Write the volume of the solution, the temperature, the time in the solution, or the size of the cubes.

worked_example.question:
A student investigates the effect of different concentrations of sugar solution on cubes of beetroot.

This is the method that they use:

Step 1 Cut four cubes of beetroot tissue.
Step 2 Place each beetroot cube in a test tube containing a different concentration of sugar solution.
Step 3 Leave the beetroot cubes in the sugar solutions for 3 hours.
Step 4 Remove the beetroot cubes from the sugar solutions.

The student wants to calculate the percentage change in mass for each beetroot cube.

They want to use the method above to collect the data they need, but have missed some steps from the method.

Describe the additional steps needed in the method to find the data.
answer_points: Use a balance to measure mass.
Measure the mass of each beetroot cube at the start of the experiment, before step 2.
Measure the mass of each beetroot cube at the end, after step 4.
Blot or dry the outside of the cubes before the final mass is measured.
worked_example.tip: Any three score one mark each.
